An '''amphidromic point''', also called a '''tidal node''', is a geographical location where there is little or no difference in sea height between high tide and low tide; it has zero tidal [[amplitude]] for one [[harmonic analysis|harmonic constituent]] of the [[tide]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Desplanque |first1=Con |last2=Mossman |first2=David J. |date=1 January 2004 |title=Tides and their seminal impact on the geology, geography, history, and socio-economics of the Bay of Fundy, eastern Canada |journal=Atlantic Geology |volume=40 |issue=1 |doi=10.4138/729 |doi-access=free}}</ref> The [[tidal range]] (the [[peak-to-peak amplitude]], or the height difference between high tide and low tide) for that harmonic constituent increases with distance from this point, though not uniformly. As such, the concept of amphidromic points is crucial to understanding tidal behaviour.<ref name="psu.edu">{{cite web|url=https://courseware.e-education.psu.edu/courses/earth540/www.e-education.psu.edu/earth540/content/c6_p1.html|title=Tides in two easy pieces - Earth 540: Essentials of Oceanography for Educators|access-date=2026-06-29|website=Penn State Department of Geosciences|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260629045730/https://courseware.e-education.psu.edu/courses/earth540/www.e-education.psu.edu/earth540/content/c6_p1.html|archive-date=2026-06-29|url-status=live}}</ref> The term derives from the [[Greek language|Greek]] words ''amphi'' ("around") and ''dromos'' ("running"), referring to the rotary tides which circulate around amphidromic points.<ref>{{Cite book | publisher = [[Cambridge University Press]] | isbn = 978-0-521-79746-7 | last = Cartwright | first = David Edgar | title = Tides: A Scientific History | year = 2000 | page = 243 }}</ref> It was first discovered by [[William Whewell]], who extrapolated the [[Cotidal line|cotidal lines]] from the coast of the [[North Sea]] and found that the lines must meet at some point.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Berry |first=Michael |date=January 2000 |title=Making waves in physics |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=403 |issue=6765 |page=21 |doi=10.1038/47364 |pmid=10638732 |bibcode=2000Natur.403...21B |s2cid=38351145 |issn=1476-4687|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Amphidromic points occur because [[Interference (wave propagation)|interference]] within [[oceanic basin]]s, [[sea]]s and bays, combined with the [[Coriolis effect]], creates a wave pattern — called an '''amphidromic system''' — which rotates around the amphidromic point.<ref name="psu.edu" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Tides |url=http://www.salemstate.edu/~lhanson/gls214/gls214_tides.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100602031717/https://www.salemstate.edu/~lhanson/gls214/gls214_tides.html |archive-date=2010-06-02 |access-date=2010-08-23}}</ref> At the amphidromic points of the dominant [[tidal constituent]], there is almost no vertical change in sea level from tidal action; that is, there is little or no difference between high tide and low tide at these locations. There can still be tidal currents since the water levels on either side of the amphidromic point are not the same. A separate amphidromic system is created by each periodic tidal component.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ffden-2.phys.uaf.edu/645fall2003_web.dir/ellie_boyce/amphidromic.htm|title=Untitled Document|access-date=21 July 2016}}</ref>

In most locations the [[Tide#Principal lunar semi-diurnal constituent|"principal lunar semi-diurnal"]], known as ''M''<sub>2</sub>, is the largest tidal constituent. [[Cotidal line]]s connect points which reach high tide at the same time and low tide at the same time. In Figure 1, the low tide lags or leads by 1 hr 2 min from its neighboring lines. Where the lines meet are amphidromes, and the tide rotates around them; for example, along the Chilean coast, and from southern Mexico to Peru, the tide propagates southward, while from Baja California to Alaska the tide propagates northward.

== Formation of amphidromic points ==
Tides are generated as a result of [[gravitational attraction]] by the [[Sun]] and [[Moon]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last1=Pugh|first1=David|title=Sea-Level Science|last2=Woodworth|first2=Philip|date=2014|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-1-139-23577-8|location=Cambridge|doi=10.1017/cbo9781139235778}}</ref> This gravitational attraction results in a [[tidal force]] that acts on the [[ocean]].<ref name=":0" /> The ocean reacts to this external forcing by generating, in particular relevant for describing tidal behaviour, [[Kelvin wave]]s and [[Sverdrup wave|Poincaré waves]] (also known as [[Sverdrup wave]]s).<ref name=":0" /> These tidal waves can be considered wide, relative to the [[Rossby radius of deformation]] (~3000&nbsp;km in the open ocean<ref name=":1" />), and shallow, as the water depth (''D'', on average ~4 kilometre deep<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last1=Charette|first1=Matthew|last2=Smith|first2=Walter|date=2010-06-01|title=The Volume of Earth's Ocean|journal=Oceanography|volume=23|issue=2|pages=112–114|doi=10.5670/oceanog.2010.51|issn=1042-8275|doi-access=free|bibcode=2010Ocgpy..23b.112C |hdl=1912/3862|hdl-access=free}}</ref>) in the ocean is much smaller (i.e. ''D''/''λ'' <1/20) than the [[wavelength]] (''λ'') which is in the order of thousands of kilometres.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Citation|last1=Toffoli|first1=Alessandro|title=Types of Ocean Surface Waves, Wave Classification|date=2017-03-06|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Maritime and Offshore Engineering|pages=1–8|place=Chichester, UK|publisher=John Wiley & Sons, Ltd|isbn=978-1-118-47635-2|last2=Bitner-Gregersen|first2=Elzbieta M.|doi=10.1002/9781118476406.emoe077}}</ref>

[[File:Nodes antinodes corrected y-axis and x-axis.jpg|thumb|386x386px|Figure 2. Resonance between an incident and reflected wave and the resulting total wave. At certain points (nodes), the amplitude of the incident wave and the reflected wave cancel each other out. At other points (antinodes), the amplitude of the incident wave and the reflected wave amplify each other. The respective distance between the nodes and antinodes are shown in the bottom right of the Figure and expressed in terms of wavelength.]]
In real oceans, the tides cannot endlessly propagate as [[progressive wave]]s. The waves reflect due to changes in water depth (for example when entering [[Continental shelf|shelf seas]]) and at coastal boundaries.<ref name=":0" /> The result is a [[Reflection (physics)|reflected]] wave that propagates in the opposite direction to the incident wave. The combination of the reflected wave and the incident wave is the total wave.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Hersey|first=J. B.|date=1961-11-03|title=Physical Oceanography. Albert Defant. Pergamon, New York, 1961. vol. 1, xvi + 729 pp.; vol. 2, viii + 598 pp. Illus. + maps. $35|journal=Science|volume=134|issue=3488|page=1412|doi=10.1126/science.134.3488.1412|issn=0036-8075}}</ref> Due to [[resonance]] between the reflected and the incident wave, the amplitude of the total wave can either be suppressed or amplified.<ref name=":0" /> The points at which the two waves amplify each other are known as [[antinodes]] and the points at which the two waves cancel each other out are known as [[Node (physics)|nodes]]. Figure 2 shows a {{frac|1|4}}λ resonator. The first node is located at {{frac|1|4}}λ of the total wave, followed by the next node reoccurring {{frac|1|2}}λ farther at {{frac|3|4}}λ.

A long, progressive wave travelling in a channel on a rotating Earth behaves differently from a wave travelling along a non-rotating channel. Due to the [[Coriolis force]], the water in the ocean is deflected towards the right in the northern hemisphere and conversely in the southern hemisphere.<ref name=":0" /> This side-way component of the flow due to the Coriolis force causes a build-up of water that results in a [[pressure gradient]].<ref name=":0" /> The resulting slope develops until it is [[Equilibrium point|equilibrium]] with the Coriolis force; resulting in [[geostrophic balance]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Phillips|first=Norman A.|date=1963|title=Geostrophic motion|journal=Reviews of Geophysics|volume=1|issue=2|pages=123–176|doi=10.1029/rg001i002p00123|bibcode=1963RvGSP...1..123P|issn=8755-1209}}</ref> As a result of this geostrophic balance, Kelvin waves (originally described by [[William Thomson, 1st Baron Kelvin|Lord Kelvin]]) and Poincaré waves are generated. The amplitude of a Kelvin wave is highest near the coast and, when considering a wave on the northern hemisphere, decreases to further away from its right-hand coastal boundary.<ref name=":1">{{Citation|last=Wang|first=B.|title=Kelvin Waves|date=2003|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Atmospheric Sciences|pages=1062–1068|publisher=Elsevier|doi=10.1016/b0-12-227090-8/00191-3|isbn=978-0-12-227090-1}}</ref> The propagation of Kelvin waves is always alongshore and its amplification falls off according to the Rossby radius of deformation.<ref name=":1" /> In contrast, Poincaré waves are able to propagate both alongshore as a free wave with a propagating wave pattern and cross-shore as a trapped wave with a [[standing wave]] pattern.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Gill |first=Aan E.  |title=Atmosphere--Ocean Dynamics. |last2=Donn |first2=William L. |date=3 June 2016 |publisher=Elsevier |isbn=978-1-4832-8158-2 |oclc=952336940}}</ref>

=== Infinitely long channel ===
In an infinitely long channel, which can be viewed upon as a simplified approximation of the [[Atlantic Ocean]] and [[Pacific Ocean]], the tide propagates as an incident and a reflective Kelvin wave<!-- as shown in Animation 1. The red coloured lines indicate high tide and the blue coloured lines indicate low tide. Furthermore, the [[Vector field|vectors field]] below the basin in Animation 1 show the direction and the strength of the tidal current -->. The amplitude of the waves decreases further away from the coast and at certain points in the middle of the basin, the amplitude of the total wave becomes zero. Moreover, the phase of the tide seems to rotate around these points of zero amplitude. These points are called amphidromic points. The sense of rotation of the wave around the amphidromic point is in the direction of the Coriolis force; anticlockwise in the [[Northern Hemisphere|northern hemisphere]] and clockwise in the [[Southern Hemisphere|southern hemisphere]].

=== Semi-enclosed basin ===

In a semi-enclosed basin, such as the North Sea, Kelvin waves, though being the dominant tidal wave propagating in alongshore direction, are not able to propagate cross shore as they rely on the presence of lateral boundaries or the [[equator]].<ref name=":1" /> As such, the tidal waves observed cross-shore are predominantly Poincaré waves. The tides observed in a semi-enclosed basin are therefore chiefly the summation of the incident Kelvin wave, reflected Kelvin wave and cross-shore standing Poincaré wave. An animation of the tidal amplitude, tidal currents and its amphidromic behaviour is shown in Animation 2.

=== Position of amphidromic points ===
Figure 2 shows that the first node of the total wave is located at {{frac|1|4}}λ with reoccurring nodes at intervals of {{frac|1|2}}λ. In an idealized situation, amphidromic points can be found at the position of these nodes of the total tidal wave.<ref name=":0" /> When neglecting friction, the position of the amphidromic points would be in the middle of the basin, as the initial amplitude and the amplitude decay of the incident wave and the reflected wave are equal, this can be seen in Animations 1 and 2<ref name=":0" />  However, tidal waves in the ocean are subject to friction from the [[seabed]] and from interaction with coastal boundaries. Moreover, variation in water depth influences the spacing between amphidromic points.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":3" />

Firstly, the distance between amphidromic points is dependent on the water depth:<ref name=":0" />

<math>\lambda=\sqrt{gD}\cdot T</math>

Where ''g'' is the [[gravitational acceleration]], ''D'' is the water depth and ''T'' is the [[Wave period|period]] of the wave.

Locations with more shallow water depth have their amphidromic points closer to each other as the distance of the interval ({{frac|1|2}}λ) of the nodes decreases. Secondly, energy losses due to friction in shallow seas and coastal boundaries result in additional adjustments of the tidal pattern.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last=Pugh|first=D. T.|date=1981-11-01|title=Tidal amphidrome movement and energy dissipation in the Irish Sea|journal=Geophysical Journal International|volume=67|issue=2|pages=515–527|doi=10.1111/j.1365-246x.1981.tb02763.x|bibcode=1981GeoJ...67..515P|issn=0956-540X|doi-access=free}}</ref> Tidal waves are not perfectly reflected, resulting in energy loss which causes a smaller reflected wave compared to the incoming wave.<ref name=":0" /> Consequently, on the northern hemisphere, the amphidromic point will be displaced from the centre line of the channel towards the left of the direction of the incident wave.<ref name=":0" />

The degree of displacement on the northern hemisphere for the first amphidrome is given by:<ref name=":0" />

<math>\gamma=-\frac{\sqrt{gD}\cdot\ln\alpha}{2f}</math>

Where γ is the displacement of the amphidrome from the centre of the channel (''γ''=0), ''g'' is the gravitational acceleration, ''D'' is the water depth, ''f'' is the [[Coriolis frequency]] and ''α'' is the ratio between amplitudes of the reflected wave and the incident wave. Because the reflected wave is smaller than the incident wave,<ref name=":0" /> ''α'' will be smaller than 1 and ''lnα'' will be negative. Hence the amphidromic displacement ''γ'' is to the left of the incident wave on the northern hemisphere.

Furthermore, a study has shown than there is a pattern of amphidrome movement related to [[Tide|spring-neap]] cycles in the [[Irish Sea]].<ref name=":2" /> The maximum displacement of the amphidrome from the centre coincides with [[spring tides]], whereas the minimum occurs at [[neaps]]. During spring tides, more energy is absorbed from the tidal wave compared to neap tides. As a result, the reflection coefficient ''α'' is smaller and the displacement of the amphidromic point from the centre is larger. Similar amphidromic movement is expected in other seas where [[energy dissipation]] due to friction is high.<ref name=":0" />

It can occur that the amphidromic point moves inland of the coastal boundary.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Murty|first1=T. S.|last2=Henry|first2=R. F.|date=1983|title=Tides in the Bay of Bengal|journal=Journal of Geophysical Research|volume=88|issue=C10|page=6069|doi=10.1029/jc088ic10p06069|bibcode=1983JGR....88.6069M|issn=0148-0227}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Sindhu|first1=B.|last2=Unnikrishnan|first2=A. S.|date=December 2013|title=Characteristics of Tides in the Bay of Bengal|journal=Marine Geodesy|volume=36|issue=4|pages=377–407|doi=10.1080/01490419.2013.781088|bibcode=2013MarGe..36..377S |s2cid=53365068|issn=0149-0419}}</ref> In this case, the amplitude and the phase of the tidal wave will still rotate around an inland point, which is called a virtual or degenerate amphidrome.

=== Amphidromic points and sea level rise ===
The position of amphidromic points and their movement predominantly depends on the wavelength of the tidal wave and friction. As a result of enhanced [[greenhouse gas emissions]], the oceans in the world are becoming subject to [[Sea level rise|sea-level rise]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cazenave |first1=Anny |author-link=Anny Cazenave |last2=Cozannet |first2=Gonéri Le |date=February 2014 |title=Sea level rise and its coastal impacts |journal=Earth's Future |volume=2 |issue=2 |pages=15–34 |doi=10.1002/2013ef000188 |bibcode=2014EaFut...2...15C|issn=2328-4277 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Church|first1=John A.|last2=White|first2=Neil J.|date=2011-03-30|title=Sea-Level Rise from the Late 19th to the Early 21st Century|journal=Surveys in Geophysics|volume=32|issue=4–5|pages=585–602|doi=10.1007/s10712-011-9119-1|bibcode=2011SGeo...32..585C|issn=0169-3298|doi-access=free}}</ref>  As the water depth increases, the wavelength of the tidal wave will increase. Consequently the position of the amphidromic points located at {{frac|1|4}}λ in semi-enclosed systems will move further away from the cross-shore coastal boundary. Furthermore, amphidromic points will move further away from each other as the interval of {{frac|1|2}}λ increases. This effect will be more pronounced in shallow seas and coastal regions, as the relative water depth increase due to sea-level rise will be larger, when compared to the open ocean. Moreover, the amount of sea-level rise differs per region.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Yin|first1=Jianjun|last2=Griffies|first2=Stephen M.|last3=Stouffer|first3=Ronald J.|date=2010-09-01|title=Spatial Variability of Sea Level Rise in Twenty-First Century Projections|journal=Journal of Climate|volume=23|issue=17|pages=4585–4607|doi=10.1175/2010jcli3533.1|bibcode=2010JCli...23.4585Y|issn=1520-0442|doi-access=free}}</ref> Some regions will be subject to a higher rate of sea-level rise than other regions and nearby amphidromic points will be more susceptible to change location. Lastly, sea-level rise results in less bottom friction and therefore less energy dissipation.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Arns|first1=Arne|last2=Dangendorf|first2=Sönke|last3=Jensen|first3=Jürgen|last4=Talke|first4=Stefan|last5=Bender|first5=Jens|last6=Pattiaratchi|first6=Charitha|date=2017-01-06|title=Sea-level rise induced amplification of coastal protection design heights|journal=Scientific Reports|volume=7|issue=1|article-number=40171|doi=10.1038/srep40171|pmid=28057920|pmc=5216410|bibcode=2017NatSR...740171A|issn=2045-2322|doi-access=free}}</ref> This causes the amphidromic points to move further away from the coastal boundaries and more towards the centre its channel/basin.

==In the ''M''<sub>2</sub> tidal constituent==
Based on Figure 1, there are the following [[clockwise]] and anticlockwise amphidromic points:[[File:Amfidromieen.JPG|thumb|right|259x259px|Figure 3. Amphidromic system of the ''M''<sub>2</sub> constituent in the [[North Sea]]. The light-blue lines are lines of equal tidal phase for the vertical tide (surface elevation) along such a line, and the amphidromic points are denoted by 1, 2 and 3.]]

=== Clockwise amphidromic points ===
* north of the [[Seychelles]]
* near [[Enderby Land]]
* off [[Perth, Western Australia|Perth]]
* east of [[New Guinea]]
* south of [[Easter Island]]
* west of the [[Galapagos Islands]]
* north of [[Queen Maud Land]]

=== Counterclockwise amphidromic points ===
* near [[Sri Lanka]]
* north of [[New Guinea]]
* at [[Tahiti]]
* between [[Mexico]] and [[Hawaii]]
* near the [[Leeward Islands]]
* east of [[Newfoundland (island)|Newfoundland]]
* midway between [[Rio de Janeiro]] and [[Angola]]
* east of [[Iceland]]
*Outside [[Eigersund Municipality|Eigersund]] in southwestern [[Norway]]<ref>[https://www.codar.com/images/about/2017SperrevikUB.pdf Modeling coastal circulation in Norway using a high-resolution 4D-Var ocean assimilation system]</ref>
* The islands of [[Madagascar]] and [[New Zealand]] are amphidromic points in the sense that the tide goes around them in about 12 and a half hours, but the amplitude of the tides on their coasts is in some places large.
